short: A Roman poet of pastoral Eclogues.
note: Titus Calpurnius Siculus is the Latin poet credited with seven Eclogues, poems that combine shepherds’ songs and rural life with praise of an emperor. Their precise date is debated.

short: A Roman geographical writer.
note: Pomponius Mela wrote De chorographia in the first century CE. This description of the lands and peoples of the known world is the earliest surviving Latin geographical treatise.

sources.label: Cambridge History of Classical Literature: Technical writing

short: Possibly Plutarch’s collection of essays and dialogues.
note: Possibly Plutarch’s Moralia, a broad collection of Greek essays and dialogues on ethics, religion, philosophy, education, and everyday customs. The conventional Latin title means moral writings.

short: A merchant who sells cloth.
note: A dealer in textiles or fabric, particularly cloth sold for making clothes.

short: Latin: “She flies with her own wings.”
note: Literally, he or she flies with his or her own wings. The feminine translation is familiar as the state motto of Oregon.

short: A traditional size of writing paper.
note: A historical paper size named for its original watermark depicting a jester’s cap. The term later became a general name for certain large sheets of writing paper.

short: Virgil, the Roman poet of the Aeneid.
note: Publius Vergilius Maro (70–19 BCE), usually called Virgil or Vergil in English, wrote the pastoral Eclogues, the agricultural Georgics, and the epic Aeneid.

short: Latin: “From the depths of the heart.”
note: Literally, from the lowest part of the breast: deeply or wholeheartedly. Classical poets use the breast as the seat of strong feeling.

short: Latin: “Experience is a teacher.”
note: Usus means practice or experience, and magister means teacher. Related ancient maxims call experience the best teacher.

short: Possibly Philostratus the Elder, author of Imagines.
note: Possibly Philostratus the Elder, the Greek author of Imagines, descriptions of paintings. Book 2.17 conducts an imagined voyage among painted islands inhabited by gods, farmers, hunters, and fabulous creatures.

term: Nobis cum semel occidit brevis lux
short: A line from Catullus’s fifth poem.
note: Catullus 5 contrasts recurring sunsets with human mortality: once our brief light ends, an unending night of sleep follows. Brevis lux is the brief light; perpetua nox is perpetual night.

short: Ovid: medicine largely depends on timing.
note: From Ovid’s Remedia amoris, line 131: medical skill is largely an art of timing. The following lines explain that wine can help when given at the right time and harm at the wrong time.

term: My boyhood saw Greek islands floating over Harvard Square
short: A quotation from Horace Gregory’s Chorus for Survival.
note: Horace Gregory’s Chorus for Survival (1935) gives these lines to Ralph Waldo Emerson, recalling an education saturated in ancient Greek culture.

sources.label: National Archives: quotation reference, printed p. 161

short: Ernest Hemingway, American novelist and short-story writer.
note: Ernest Hemingway (1899–1961) wrote The Sun Also Rises, A Farewell to Arms, and The Old Man and the Sea. His prose is associated with compression, restrained description, and omission.

short: Rudyard Kipling, author of The Jungle Book and Kim.
note: Rudyard Kipling (1865–1936) was a British poet and storyteller whose works include The Jungle Book, Kim, and Just So Stories.

short: Possibly Dorothy Parker, American humorist and writer.
note: Possibly Dorothy Parker (1893–1967), whose short stories, verse, criticism, and epigrams are known for their sharp wit. She was associated with the Algonquin Round Table.

sources.label: Academy of American Poets: Dorothy Parker

short: James Thurber, American humorist and cartoonist.
note: James Thurber (1894–1961) wrote comic stories and drew cartoons, many published in The New Yorker. His works include The Secret Life of Walter Mitty.

short: Possibly John Crowley, the fantasy novelist.
note: Possibly John Crowley, the American novelist whose books include Little, Big, a fantasy about a family’s entanglement with the realm of fairies.

short: W. H. Hudson, writer and naturalist.
note: William Henry Hudson (1841–1922) was an Argentine-born British writer and naturalist. His books include the novel Green Mansions and essays on birds, animals, and the countryside.

sources.label: W. H. Hudson: The Book of a Naturalist

short: W. H. Hudson’s 1904 romance.
note: Green Mansions: A Romance of the Tropical Forest is W. H. Hudson’s novel about a traveler’s encounter with Rima in the forests of South America.

short: A collection of W. H. Hudson’s nature essays.
note: Hudson’s The Book of a Naturalist gathers observations and reflections on animals, birds, human relationships with nature, and the English countryside.

sources.label: W. H. Hudson: The Book of a Naturalist

short: The “kindly ones,” a propitiatory name for the Furies.
note: Eumenides means the kindly or gracious ones in Greek. It is a reassuring name for the Erinyes, terrifying powers who punish wrongdoing, especially crimes against kin.

short: The square relation for a right triangle.
note: In a right triangle, the square of the hypotenuse equals the sum of the squares of the two other sides: a² + b² = c². Euclid proves the result in Elements I.47.

short: An ancient Greek philosopher associated with number and harmony.
note: Pythagoras of Samos, active in the sixth century BCE, founded a religious and philosophical community in southern Italy. Later traditions connect him with mathematical number relations and musical harmony.

short: Latin: “Peace in war.”
note: Pax means peace; in bello means in war or during war.

sources.label: Lewis and Short Latin Dictionary: pax

short: Hawthorne’s retellings of Greek myths for children.
note: Nathaniel Hawthorne’s A Wonder-Book for Girls and Boys (1851) retells six Greek myths, including Bellerophon and Pegasus in The Chimæra.

sources.label: Nathaniel Hawthorne: A Wonder Book for Girls & Boys

short: The Greek hero who rode Pegasus against the Chimera.
note: Bellerophon is a hero of Greek mythology who masters the winged horse Pegasus and is sent to kill the fire-breathing Chimera.

short: The winged horse of Greek mythology.
note: Pegasus springs from Medusa after her death and becomes Bellerophon’s mount. Ancient accounts also associate him with the Muses and a spring on Mount Helicon.

short: A fire-breathing composite monster of Greek myth.
note: The Chimera combines features of a lion, goat, and serpent. Bellerophon defeats it while riding Pegasus. The name later became a word for a fantastic hybrid or impossible imagining.

short: Lucretius: “Victory raises us to heaven.”
note: From De rerum natura 1.79. Lucretius celebrates Epicurus’s intellectual victory over oppressive religious fear, saying that this victory makes humanity equal to heaven.

short: William Hickling Prescott, historian of the Spanish conquests.
note: William Hickling Prescott (1796–1859) was an American historian best known for his histories of the Spanish conquests of Mexico and Peru. His History of the Conquest of Mexico appeared in 1843.

sources.label: William H. Prescott: History of the Conquest of Mexico

short: An adaptation of a saying recorded by Pliny.
note: Pliny the Younger’s Letters 3.5.10 reports his uncle’s belief that no book was so bad that some part of it could not be useful. The Latin here is a variant of that saying.

short: Virgil: “Time takes everything, even the mind.”
note: Eclogue 9.51 introduces an aging singer’s lament for his lost memory and voice. Aetas means age or time, and animum can mean mind or spirit.

short: The bull-headed monster in the Cretan labyrinth.
note: In Greek mythology the Minotaur is a creature with a human body and a bull’s head, confined in the labyrinth built for King Minos and killed by Theseus.

short: The princess who helped Theseus escape the labyrinth.
note: Ariadne, daughter of King Minos of Crete, supplies Theseus with a thread by which to retrace his path after confronting the Minotaur.

short: A ball of thread; the older form behind “clue.”
note: Originally a ball of thread. The modern sense of clue developed from the idea of a thread that guides someone through a maze.

short: A low neckline, or the exposed upper chest.
note: From French décolletage: the neckline of a low-cut dress, or the neck, shoulders, and upper chest it reveals.

short: Augustine’s spiritual autobiography.
note: Augustine of Hippo’s Confessions, written around 397–400, recounts his early life and conversion to Christianity, and reflects on memory, time, and creation.

term: Notitia linguarum est prima porta sapientiae
short: Latin: “Knowledge of languages is the first gate of wisdom.”
note: A statement in Roger Bacon’s Opus tertium emphasizing the importance of learning languages for access to theology and philosophy. Notitia linguarum means knowledge of languages.

sources.label: Oxford University Press: Roger Bacon’s statement on languages

short: Horace: “Education develops innate power.”
note: From Horace’s Odes 4.4.33. Doctrina means instruction or training; vis insita is the strength already planted within a person. The next line connects sound cultivation with strengthening the heart.

short: John Ruskin’s study of Greek myth and Athena.
note: The Queen of the Air (1869) is John Ruskin’s interpretation of Greek myths as expressions of natural and spiritual meaning, centered on Athena.

sources.label: John Ruskin: The Queen of the Air

short: Roman god of the sea.
note: The Roman sea god identified with Greek Poseidon, conventionally shown with a trident.

short: Roman god of war.
note: A major Roman god associated with warfare, the protection of the Roman state, and the legendary ancestry of Rome through his sons Romulus and Remus.

short: Greek goddess of wisdom, crafts, and warfare.
note: Athena is the patron goddess of Athens, associated with practical intelligence, weaving and other crafts, and disciplined warfare. Her Roman counterpart is Minerva.

short: The wealthy king of Lydia defeated by Cyrus.
note: Croesus ruled Lydia in the sixth century BCE. His celebrated wealth and his fall to Cyrus of Persia made his name proverbial; Herodotus recounts the oracles surrounding his defeat.

short: Hannibal’s major victory over Rome in 216 BCE.
note: At Cannae in southern Italy, Hannibal’s Carthaginian army encircled and destroyed a much larger Roman army during the Second Punic War.

short: Gaius Terentius Varro, Roman consul at Cannae.
note: Gaius Terentius Varro was one of the two Roman consuls commanding at Cannae in 216 BCE. He survived the defeat and withdrew to Venusia with a small body of cavalry.

short: The ancient Roman town now called Venosa.
note: An ancient town and Roman colony in southern Italy, now Venosa. Survivors of the Roman defeat at Cannae gathered there.

short: The Carthaginian commander in the Second Punic War.
note: Hannibal Barca led a Carthaginian army into Italy over the Alps and won major victories against Rome, including Cannae in 216 BCE.

short: Roman dictator appointed after the defeat at Cannae.
note: Marcus Junius Pera was appointed dictator in 216 BCE after Cannae. Emergency measures under his command included enrolling thousands of slaves willing to fight.

short: Virgil: “And there at last he rested in peaceful death.”
note: Aeneid 9.445, describing the death of Nisus beside his companion Euryalus. Placida morte means peaceful death; demum means at last.
